concept.name: Dealer
concept.definition: Under Section 3(a)(5)(A) of the U.S. Securities Exchange Act of 1934, a dealer is any person engaged in the business of buying and selling securities for his own account, through a broker or otherwise. Unlike a broker, who acts as agent, a dealer acts as principal and typically holds inventory, earning the bid-ask spread rather than commissions.
concept.intuition: A dealer is like a used-car lot: it owns an inventory of securities and makes money by buying low (at the bid) and selling high (at the ask) out of that inventory.
concept.mechanics: A dealer holds itself out as willing to buy and sell particular securities on a continuous basis, quotes two-sided prices, and carries inventory risk between purchases and sales. The Exchange Act 'dealer' definition excludes the 'trader' — a person who buys and sells for his own account but not as part of a regular business. Most dealers must register with the SEC and join an SRO.
concept.failure_modes: Inventory risk can produce large losses in fast markets, and dealers may widen quotes or withdraw liquidity precisely when it is most needed. Dealers trading against customers as principal face inherent conflicts of interest over pricing and markups.
concept.misconceptions: Anyone who frequently trades their own account is not automatically a 'dealer' in the legal sense — regular business activity and holding oneself out to the public are the distinguishing tests. 'Dealer' and 'trader' are distinct under the Exchange Act.
concept.example: A bond dealer quotes a corporate bond at 99.00 bid / 99.50 offer, buys 500 bonds at the bid from a seller, and later sells them from inventory at the offer, earning the half-point spread while bearing interim price risk.

citations.source: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration
